subject: paediatrics
title: Childhood Tuberculosis, Mantoux Testing and Paediatric HIV

steps.tx: Primary tuberculous infection in paediatric hosts differs fundamentally from post-primary adult disease. In children, **childhood pulmonary tuberculosis** represents primary progressive disease following inhalation of aerosolized Mycobacterium tuberculosis from an adult contact. Rather than upper lobe apical cavitation, young children develop the primary Ghon complex, consisting of a peripheral subpleural parenchymal focus, regional lymphangitis, and massive hilar lymphadenopathy, with high risks of haematogenous dissemination.
steps.say: Childhood tuberculosis presents as primary disease with a subpleural Ghon focus and marked hilar lymphadenopathy rather than apical cavities. Paucibacillary infection carries high dissemination risks.

steps.tx: Delayed-type hypersensitivity testing provides objective evidence of tuberculous infection. The **Mantoux tuberculin test** involves intradermal injection of 0.1 mL of purified protein derivative (5 TU) into the volar forearm, producing a discrete wheal that is measured across its transverse induration at forty-eight to seventy-two hours. An induration of ten millimetres or greater is positive in healthy children, whereas five millimetres or greater is positive in children with HIV, severe malnutrition, or household contacts.
steps.say: The Mantoux test measures transverse induration at forty-eight to seventy-two hours. Ten millimetres is positive in healthy children, while five millimetres is positive in HIV or malnutrition.

steps.tx: Because young children swallow sputum, specialized specimen collection recovers swallowed bronchial secretions. Performing **early morning gastric aspirates** on three consecutive mornings before the child awakens or feeds recovers overnight swallowed respiratory mucus from the stomach. Gastric lavage fluid is immediately neutralized with sodium bicarbonate and subjected to cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification testing (CBNAAT / GeneXpert MTB/RIF) to confirm Mycobacterium tuberculosis and detect rifampicin resistance.
steps.say: Early morning gastric aspirates collected on three consecutive mornings recover swallowed sputum in young children. Neutralized fluid is tested with GeneXpert for tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance.

steps.tx: First-line paediatric chemotherapy utilizes weight-banded fixed-dose combination formulations. Standard treatment for **pediatric pulmonary tuberculosis** consists of a two-month intensive phase with four drugs: isoniazid (H), rifampicin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), and ethambutol (E), followed by a four-month continuation phase with isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol (2HRZE / 4HRE). Daily administration using dispersible, flavoured tablets dramatically enhances compliance and prevents treatment failure.
steps.say: Treat paediatric pulmonary tuberculosis with two months of four drugs: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by four months of three drugs.

steps.tx: Vertical mother-to-child transmission represents the overwhelming source of pediatric retroviral infection. Effective **prevention of vertical HIV transmission** (PMTCT) requires maternal lifelong triple-drug antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, lamivudine, dolutegravir) initiated during antenatal care to achieve complete viral suppression. The infant receives prophylactic oral zidovudine and nevirapine for six to twelve weeks, which reduces mother-to-child transmission rates to under two percent.
steps.say: Preventing vertical HIV transmission requires maternal lifelong triple antiretroviral therapy. The infant receives oral zidovudine and nevirapine for six to twelve weeks, dropping transmission under two percent.

steps.tx: Transplacental maternal IgG antibodies necessitate early molecular virological assays in infants. Because maternal antibodies persist in infant serum for up to eighteen months, standard antibody ELISA tests cannot diagnose infant infection. Definitive early infant diagnosis requires **HIV DNA PCR testing** at six weeks of age, followed by repeat testing at six months and six weeks after complete cessation of breastfeeding, confirming infection only when viral nucleic acid is directly detected.
steps.say: Maternal antibodies persist for eighteen months, making antibody tests unreliable in infants. Early diagnosis requires HIV DNA PCR testing at six weeks of life.

steps.tx: Universal antibiotic prophylaxis prevents lethal opportunistic pulmonary infections in exposed infants. Beginning at six weeks of age, all HIV-exposed infants receive daily **cotrimoxazole prophylaxis** (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) to protect against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, toxoplasmosis, and severe bacterial pneumonias. Prophylaxis is continued uninterrupted until the child is confirmed HIV-uninfected after complete cessation of all breastfeeding, or continued indefinitely if the child is infected.
steps.say: Daily cotrimoxazole prophylaxis begins at six weeks for all HIV-exposed infants to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia. It continues until HIV infection is definitively excluded after weaning.

steps.tx: Rapid initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy restores immunocompetence and normal growth. All infants and children confirmed with HIV require immediate **pediatric antiretroviral therapy** regardless of CD4 count or clinical staging. Preferred first-line regimens utilize weight-banded dolutegravir dispersible tablets combined with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (abacavir plus lamivudine), which rapidly suppresses viral load and allows immune reconstitution.
steps.say: Start antiretroviral therapy immediately upon HIV diagnosis regardless of CD4 count. Preferred first-line therapy combines dolutegravir with abacavir and lamivudine dispersible tablets.
